conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m Dr. Harper, one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians here. Congratulations on your new baby—this is such a huge transition, and I’m glad we have a chance to check in on how you’re doing emotionally.

Over the next few minutes I’d like to complete the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question screen that helps us spot common mood and anxiety symptoms that can show up any time in the first year after birth. Your answers are completely confidential; the goal is simply to make sure you’re getting the support you deserve. We’ll go one question at a time, thinking about how you’ve felt in the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Looking back over the past week, have you still been able to enjoy the things you used to look forward to, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped?

I’ve still been enjoying things, actually. When the baby naps I’ll put on a podcast I like or flip through a cooking magazine, and I still get excited about little stuff like that. My enjoyment hasn’t slipped at all.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I’ve been laughing—probably not as loudly or as often as before the baby, but when my husband makes a goofy face while changing a diaper or when the dog sniffs the baby’s foot and does that confused head-tilt, I still chuckle. It hasn’t disappeared.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I do find myself looking forward to little things—like tomorrow morning’s coffee or the walk we usually take to the park. They’re small, but they still feel nice to anticipate.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really. If the baby’s extra fussy I might think, “Maybe I missed a cue,” but I don’t stay stuck on it. I figure babies just have rough spells and move on.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little bit, yeah. Sometimes I’ll suddenly wonder if the baby’s breathing okay in the bassinet, even though I just checked and he’s fine. It’s not constant—just random moments where my mind jumps to the worst for a second.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I haven’t had any real panic feelings—no racing heart or sense that something awful is about to happen. Just those quick little “what-if” worries, then I remind myself he’s okay and I calm right back down.
Things have been getting on top of me

Mostly I feel like I’m staying afloat. There are moments—like when the baby’s crying and the laundry’s piled up—where I think, “Whoa, a lot is happening,” but I take a breath, tackle one thing, and it passes.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, my sleep’s been fine. Once I finally lie down, I’m out pretty quickly—even if it’s only for a few hours before the next feeding.
I have felt sad or miserable
I haven’t felt truly sad or miserable. A little tired and stretched, sure, but not down in the dumps—more like “normal-new-mom” weary than anything heavy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I really haven’t cried much at all. Maybe once when I was extra tired and the baby wouldn’t settle, but it was brief—just a couple of tears—and then I felt fine again.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 7: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – EPDS-style self-report (10 items)

**Symptoms endorsed**  
- Transient, situational worry about infant safety (items 4, 5) – no persistent apprehension or panic attacks  
- Occasional feeling that “a lot is happening” (item 6) – resolves with simple coping, no sense of being overwhelmed  
- No sustained low mood, anhedonia, guilt, sleep-mood link, crying spells, or self-harm ideation (items 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9, 10)

**Pattern**  
Overall emotional tone: stable, reactive to normal new-mom stressors; pleasure and laughter preserved; no cognitive distortions or safety concerns.

**Screening significance**  
Current responses do not indicate probable major postpartum depression or anxiety disorder; risk profile low. Continue routine perinatal monitoring; re-screen if clinical picture changes.
